stories.title: Amit's Cycling Background
stories.description: Amit confesses he cannot ride a bicycle, attributing it to a privileged childhood with a car and later relying on public transport in Mumbai. His passion for the sport is purely intellectual.

stories.title: Rahul Dravid in the Office
stories.description: Ajay recounts playing office cricket with Rahul Dravid using a 'squeezy ball'. After Ajay bowled a wide and then clean bowled Dravid twice, Dravid jokingly said, 'Fuck you, Shoaib Akhtar, I'm not playing with you' and threw the bat.

stories.title: Primož Roglič's Skiing Accident
stories.description: The story of Primož Roglič, who was a ski jumper until a horrific crash in 2007. He switched to cycling late and became a world-class rider, showing incredible resilience.

stories.title: Roglič vs. Pogačar 2020
stories.description: In the 2020 Tour de France, Roglič was the favorite and led until the final time trial. Pogačar produced a miraculous performance to win. Roglič, despite his heartbreak, hugged and congratulated Pogačar, showing immense sportsmanship.

stories.title: Sep Kuss at the Vuelta
stories.description: During the Vuelta a España, Jumbo-Visma's domestique Sep Kuss unexpectedly took the lead. Despite having team leaders Roglič and Vingegaard in contention, the team eventually supported Kuss to win the Grand Tour.

stories.title: Wout van Aert vs. Remco Evenepoel
stories.description: A story of Belgian rivalry where Evenepoel was asked to work for Van Aert in a World Championship, felt he could have won, and then proceeded to win the World Championship the very next day.

core_ideas.description: Cycling is a team sport because of physics. Riding in someone's slipstream saves ~30% energy, meaning the person in front does the hard work while the one behind rests.

Breakaways involve a 'prisoner's dilemma'. Riders must cooperate to build a lead but become selfish enemies near the finish line. If no one chases an attacker because they want to save energy for the sprint, the attacker wins.
Dave Brailsford's philosophy that transformed British cycling: improving every small detail (diet, sleep, aerodynamics) by 1% leads to a massive cumulative advantage.
Physics (body weight) dictates roles: Climbers are light (high power-to-weight), Sprinters are heavy (explosive power), and Rouleurs are engines for the flats.
While body type (nature) determines potential, training, strategy, and 'suffering' (nurture) determine success.
Amit argues that modern cycling is largely clean compared to the EPO era, thanks to biological passports and better policing.
